newsitem.title: USA: Dole may risk all in debate by attacking Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Dole may risk all in debate by attacking Clinton.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

Republican Bob Dole and President Bill Clinton prepared for their last campaign debate on Wednesday with Dole, far behind and running out of time, apparently ready to risk all by attacking Clinton's ethics.

"Even a stellar performance tonight should not change the race very much because Dole has not offered voters a compelling reason to fire Clinton," said political scientist John Pitney at California's Claremont McKenna College.
The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Dole trimming Clinton's lead slightly to 12.8 percentage points. Other polls put the president between nine and 17 points ahead.
For Dole that is better than the 20-point deficits in some recent polls but, even so, no one has ever been this far back at this stage of a U.S. presidential campaign and won.
"He needs a powerful showing tonight ... It has got to be one heck of a show," Reuters pollster John Zogby said.
Some senior Dole advisers have been pressing him to hit the president with everything he has in Wednesday's second and final televised debate in this southern California seaport.
Dole suggested in a campaign speech on Tuesday that he means to do just that, saying he would not question Clinton's personal life but his public record was fair game.
He ticked off a list of what he calls examples of ethical faults of the Clinton administration.

He claimed 30 officials were under investigation or had resigned because of improprieties, noted that White House security officials had improperly collected FBI personal files on Republicans and claimed Clinton aides had suppressed an FBI report critical of the president's anti-drugs policies.
Dole also alleged that Clinton's Democrats had accepted huge campaign contributions from Asian businessmen seeking political access and influence over U.S. foreign policy.
"The goal is always to conceal ethical failure, not confront it," Dole said. "We hear not apologies but alibis."

Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said Dole's attacks would backfire if he tried them in the debate because voters did not like bitter negative attacks and Dole already had an image for being mean.
Presidential spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters Clinton would "respond effectively to attacks ... but move effectively to (discuss) a positive agenda for the future."
Clinton arrived in San Diego mid-morning and briefly toured the debate site on the campus of the University of San Diego before retiring to a hotel to rest.
McCurry said: "This is an important moment in the campaign, so he's treating it seriously."

Dole may indeed find it hard to carry out his threat in the 90-minute debate at the University of San Diego, where the questions were to be posed by an audience of 120 undecided voters chosen at random for the occasion.
Clinton is a master of that kind of forum, and the questions may not suit Dole's strategy in any case.

Clinton entered the debate knowing he merely had to avoid mistakes -- as he did in the first debate, on Oct. 6, when most viewers called him the winner -- to hold his commanding position for the last 20 days until the Nov. 5 election.
One issue that did come up in the first debate was Clinton's refusal to rule out pardons for associates enmeshed in criminal proceedings arising from the Whitewater land deal.

One senior Clinton campaign official said it was possible Clinton would have a response for Dole if he raised that issue again. Clinton could point out that former independent prosecutor Lawrence Walsh accuses Dole of having pushed hard for former President George Bush to pardon Republicans accused of wrongdoing in the Iran-contra scandal in the 1980s.
It remained to be seen how big a national audience their final confrontation would attract in any case.

The TV audience for the first debate was estimated at about 46 million viewers, 34 percent fewer than watched the comparable 1992 debate. In addition, Wednesday's debate was competing against a professional baseball playoff game televised on one of the major networks.
